---
title: "A5 self-check — Signalling and integration"
---

Explain each mechanism before opening its answer. Refer to the
[tutorial](index.qmd) for a connected account.

## 1. Does a sodium channel pump sodium against its gradient using ATP?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. A channel allows ions to move down their electrochemical driving force.
ATP-dependent transport maintains gradients over time. Channel opening and
active transport are different mechanisms.
:::

## 2. How can a stronger stimulus be represented without taller action potentials?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Firing frequency, timing and recruitment of additional neurons can change.
Individual spikes remain approximately stereotyped under comparable conditions.
Encoding depends on receptor and circuit properties.
:::

## 3. What connects a presynaptic action potential to transmitter release at a typical chemical synapse?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Voltage-dependent calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal promotes vesicle
release. The transmitter then acts on postsynaptic receptors; the receptor
and cell's state determine the effect.
:::

## 4. Does zero external work during a stationary hold imply zero ATP use?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. With no displacement, the simple external $Fd$ work is zero, but force
maintenance and ion handling can consume ATP. Mechanical output is not the
entire metabolic expenditure.
:::

## 5. Must equal circulating hormone concentrations cause equal responses in all tissues?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. Receptors, downstream pathways, hormone access, breakdown and sensitivity
can differ. A signal concentration is one component of a response mechanism.
:::

## 6. Is all mammalian reproductive feedback negative?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. Negative feedback contributes to regulation, but appropriate sustained
oestrogen signalling can promote positive feedback before an LH surge. The
sign depends on physiological context and timing; the loop is not an endlessly
amplifying event.
:::
